newsitem.title: FRANCE: Zeroual closes economy talks, vows to protect welfare.
newsitem.headline: Zeroual closes economy talks, vows to protect welfare.

text.p: Algeria's President Liamine Zeroual on Thursday wound up five days of talks on ways to restore the nation's battered industry, in debate marked by frankness on past mismanagement and fears and hope for the future.

Zeroual, whose country has been scarred by violence blamed on Moslem fundamentalists and sabotage estimated at $2 billion, had summoned 500 people to give ideas on salvaging industry which works at only 35 percent capacity yet employs 1.7 million of the five million strong workforce.

In remarks carried by the Algerian media, he said he was convinced the country would soon see an economic take-off and durable development but said the country could not envisage economic development without social objectives.
Diplomats have long said that Algerian industry, outside the oil and gas sector, was overmanned, inefficient and producing expensive products no-one wanted.
Officials have also expressed worry that mass layoffs, seen as needed to kickstart industry, would send recruits to Moslem radicals fighting to topple the government.

Algeria's oil and gas industry was off-limits for debate. It earns around 10 billion a year -- more than 95 percent of all foreign earnings. This compares with enterprises run as state fiefdoms since Algerian independence in 1962.
At stake are some 400 public companies which have in the past seven years had about 500 billion dinars (9 billion) pumped into them, with continued poor results.

In the first half of 1996 industrial production fell seven percent compared with the same period last year. Earnings went up, from exports like small harvesters to places like Iraq, and dates, wine and scrap material.
These exports earned just $366 million in the first quarter of 1996. And this was a 53.4 percent rise over the same period the year before.
"It seems imperative that Algerian industry manages, by itself, to release the resources for its own development," business confederation leader Said Nait Abdellaziz said.
His comments were reported by Algerian state media.
Nait Abdellaziz said that within these 400 groups were some 33,300 specialist, medium and small, firms employing 1.2 million workers, or 30 percent of the workforce.

Treasury director general Mohamed Younsi told the meeting that public firms had not repaid either the treasury, or the banks, and in 1992, 1995 and 1996 there were major operations to help the companies
"Moreover, the treasury had bought back company bank debts. Besides the 670 billion dinars this cost, the treasury also disbursed 550 billion dinars," he said.
Delegates offered privatisation as one hope for the future -- but fears of job losses brought a warning from the UGTA trades union that it would always defend jobs.

The voice of the old-guard National Liberation Front (FLN), which ruled for three decades of socialism until 1991, also echoed through the hall. "The total and rapid abandonment of this sector would be a suicidal solution," its spokesman was quoted as saying by the official news agency APS.
Algeria last week announced a privatisation council and delegates called for more encouragement for foreign investors.
But outside over 30 contracts signed with the state oil and gas giant Sonatrach there has been little sign of foreign interest in this.
Other delegates saw Algeria's rescheduling of $12 billion of its estimated $32 billion foreign debt as giving a breather to reorganise industry and management training.

A speaker for the legal Moslem fundamentalist party Hamas blamed lack of a national strategy for managing the debt. "The economic problem will remain, for earnings will go inexorably in serving the debt," he said.
Algeria teetered near bankruptcy in 1994 when energy earnings were 8.4 billion and repayments without rescheduling would have totalled 9 billion.
Rescheduling brought debt serving down to 42 percent of earnings in 1995 and to 33 percent last year. But one senior Western diplomat said last week they would now start to rise.
